The problem

Unreal's markerless mocap pipeline has no batching

MetaHuman Animator handles one single take at a time. Every clip means, after importing via Live Link/Capture Manager, manually adding it and processing it through MetaHuman Animator. Fine for a couple of hero shots. Painful for a real shoot day with a hundred takes to get through afterward.

What it does

Already built, already running

01

Drop footage straight in

No manual import step first. Point it at a folder of markerless mocap footage and it takes it from there.

02

Naming, handled

On import, it flags a shot/take naming mistake and shows you the suggested fix before anything actually gets renamed.

03

Character manager

Add your MetaHuman to Call Sheet's character list, then set face, body, and foot-lock, per take or as a blanket for the whole batch, all from inside Call Sheet.

04

Unattended batching

Every take runs through MetaHuman Animator on its own. No standing over it clicking process, one take at a time.

Proof, not a pitch

Built on a real production

Call Sheet is built and tested against real mocap takes from "Do You Copy?," not developed in the abstract.

The panel alongside is Call Sheet actually batching takes from the film's shoot, real footage, not a staged demo. That's where its real pitfalls get found and fixed, not just anticipated.

The film

Do You Copy?

Pavel Balakin is a flight engineer aboard a failing Soviet space station, rationing power, food, and company as the ground below him goes quiet. The one voice that still gets through is Kat, back home. As his supplies run out and the silence stretches on, staying in contact with her becomes the only mission that still matters.

Loosely inspired by the real cosmonauts left in orbit as the Soviet Union dissolved beneath them, cut off from a state that stopped answering, unsure what they'd be coming home to. "Do You Copy?" isn't a retelling of any one of their stories. It borrows the premise and asks a smaller, more personal question: what isolation does to the person still trying to reach you, and to the one who can't stop trying to answer.

Draft 04 Script locked, written by Aidan Martin & Phil Lemon

What's next

Speed and reach

Right now Call Sheet runs on one machine. The next four stretches take it from a tool that works for me to one another production could actually pick up.

Q1

Harden & validate

Stress-test the existing batch processor against real edge cases: mixed take types, retakes, partial batches, error recovery. Run a full time-saved pass against "Do You Copy?" takes, measured against the old manual workflow.

Q2

Network job queue

Split shot and take processing across separate nodes on a render farm, so a big batch runs in parallel instead of grinding through one machine in sequence. Not about babysitting less, about real throughput.

Q3

Standalone take manager

A take management interface that runs outside Unreal entirely, plus a general polish and hardening pass, the setup friction and edge cases that matter once it's not just running on my machine.

Q4

Open source release

Ship Call Sheet v1, get it in front of a few other small or indie MetaHuman productions, and iterate on real feedback. "Do You Copy?" keeps using it as its own pipeline tool throughout.

In development

Footage to Previs Scene

Footage to Previs Scene turns existing reference material into an editable 3D previsualisation scene. It's the first pipeline built beyond MetaHuman Animator. Body and camera tracking are recovered from ordinary mono video with SAM3D and GVHMR, no volume or suit required, arriving in Maya as a rigged, skinned character with its facial animation intact. An edit assembled in Premiere carries across as a camera sequence, so the cut drives the previs rather than being rebuilt after it. Every component can run on a closed network.

Further out, no committed timeline

The dream

An integrated production suite

Call Sheet becomes the spine of a full production management suite: scheduling, media, shot tracking, and dailies running as one system, not six disconnected apps.

Optical tracking

An open source optical system

A marker-based optical tracking system to sit alongside the markerless pipeline, for productions that need higher-fidelity capture than a single camera can give. Built and released in the open rather than licensed from a commercial rig.
